units.title: Cardiac Action Potentials and Vaughan Williams Classification
units.sec: Cardiac Action Potentials and Vaughan Williams Classification · p69
units.guide: Part 1 starts from the action potential: myocardial cells contract and eject blood after an action potential, while the SA node spontaneously depolarizes to generate heart rate. Myocardial depolarization is Na+-driven, the plateau uses K+, Ca2+ and inward Na+ channels, and repolarization uses delayed-rectifier K+. The first antiarrhythmic map is Vaughan Williams: class I targets Na+ channels, class II β receptors, class III K+ channels, class IV Ca2+ channels and class V miscellaneous agents.

units.title: SVT/PSVT Pathology and AV Nodal Treatment Preference
units.sec: SVT/PSVT Pathology and AV Nodal Treatment Preference · p70
units.guide: SVT/PSVT is explained as a fast atrial rhythm driving AV nodal action, increasing ventricular rate and risking incomplete ventricular contraction, ventricular fibrillation and arrest. The treatment aim is to block the AV node. Adenosine is the IV DOC for acute management, β blockers such as esmolol/metoprolol are limited by bronchoconstriction, diltiazem/verapamil cover acute and long-term management, and oral digoxin is for long-term management.

units.title: Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter and Ventricular Arrhythmia Strategy
units.sec: Atrial Fibrillation/Flutter and Ventricular Arrhythmia Strategy · p70
units.guide: For atrial fibrillation/flutter, abnormal rate and disrupted rhythm come most commonly from ectopic functional atrial circuits. Management is split into ventricular rate control under 100 bpm by AV node block and rhythm control by blocking ectopic myocardial cells. Cardioversion is the treatment of choice acutely, β blockers are long-term DOC for rate control, and amiodarone is DOC among rhythm-control K+ blockers; ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation is treated by blocking myocardial cells, especially with amiodarone.

units.title: Class I Na+ Channel Blocker Classification and Electrophysiology
units.sec: Class I Na+ Channel Blocker Classification and Electrophysiology · p71
units.guide: Class I drugs are divided into Ia, Ib and Ic. Ia drugs have intermediate Na+ blockade, open-state binding, significant K+ block, QT prolongation, maximum repolarization delay and prolonged PR; Ib drugs have very short closed-state blockade, K+ opening, QT shortening and normal AV/PR effects; Ic drugs have very long open-state blockade, maximum depolarization delay, normal QT and prolonged PR by blocking AP propagation.

units.title: Class Ia Drugs: Uses, Routes and Toxicities
units.sec: Class Ia Drugs: Uses, Routes and Toxicities · p72
units.guide: Class Ia drugs are second-line rhythm-control drugs for atrial fibrillation/flutter and ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation. Quinidine is oral and classically causes torsades, diarrhea and α-block hypotension; procainamide is IV and causes ganglionic-block hypotension, leukopenia/infections, agranulocytosis and SLE; disopyramide is oral and anticholinergic, causing urinary retention, mydriasis, dry mouth, constipation and PR shortening by AV nodal stimulation.

units.title: Class Ib Drugs: Lidocaine, Mexiletine and Phenytoin
units.sec: Class Ib Drugs: Lidocaine, Mexiletine and Phenytoin · p72
units.guide: Lidocaine targets ischemic and digoxin-toxic ventricular tissue because persistently depolarized cells keep Na+ channels closed long enough for closed-state blockade. It is IV because of high first-pass metabolism, contraindicated/ineffective in atrial arrhythmias with small action potentials, and causes neurologic toxicity such as nystagmus, paresthesia and seizures. Mexiletine is the oral lidocaine derivative, and phenytoin is the antiepileptic Na+ blocker used for digoxin-induced ventricular tachycardia.

units.title: Class Ic Drugs and WPW Syndrome
units.sec: Class Ic Drugs and WPW Syndrome · p73
units.guide: Class Ic drugs are strongest Na+ blockers, and flecainide is the key named drug. In WPW syndrome, flecainide is DOC because blocking Na+ and K+ channels maximally increases refractory period in both normal cells and the accessory pathway. Pure AV nodal blockers such as digoxin, β blockers and CCBs are contraindicated in WPW because they increase conduction through the accessory pathway.
